documentation.range: The Bluespotted Lagoon Ray is widespread throughout the Indo-West Pacific from South Africa to Papua New Guinea (Last et al. 2016).
documentation.population:
There are no data on the absolute population size of the Bluespotted Lagoon Ray. The species is considered common on reefs throughout Indonesia, Malaysia, Papua New Guinea, the Red Sea, Tanzania, and Madagascar but is considered scarce through the rest of its range (Fahmi unpubl. data 2020, C. Simpfendorfer unpubl. data 2020).

Spatial variation in an index of population abundance was constructed from the Global Finprint project that sampled in nations containing 93.1% of the coral reefs within the Bluespotted Lagoon Ray’s known range from 2015 to 2018. This is the largest data set available to assess the status of this species. The analysis estimate population level by reef by comparing local abundance indices to a level inferred to represent no depletion. Reef level depletion estimates were aggregated by jurisdiction and weighted by jurisdictional coral reef area (relative to global coral reef area) to produce an estimate of global relative population level. The coral reef area weighted population increase of Bluespotted Lagoon Ray was estimated as 151.2% (standard error 104.6 – 197.9%) and assumed to have occurred over the past three generation lengths (29 years) (see Supplementary Information). Therefore, based on the Finprint data, the Bluespotted Lagoon Ray meets the criteria for Least Concern. 

There is evidence that the population increase observed in Southeast Asia is related to a decrease in shark presence due to overfishing (Sherman et al. 2020), and it is a relatively productive species biologically, therefore it has not declined like other species have in the region. However, with continued fishing pressure on elasmobranchs, this species may experience population declines in the future.
documentation.habitats: The Bluespotted Lagoon Ray is benthic on inshore reefs to a depth of 50 m (Last et al. 2016, Weigmann 2016). It lives primarily around coral reefs, sheltering under ledges and in caves during the day (Last et al. 2016). It reaches a maximum size of 35 cm disc width (DW), males mature at 20 cm DW and female size-at-maturity is unknown (Last et al. 2016). Reproduction is viviparous and size-at-birth is 13–14 cm DW (Last et al. 2016). Little else is known of its biology. Generation length is inferred from the similar sized Coral Sea Maskray (Neotrygon trigonoides), which has similar distribution and a generation length of 9.7 years (Pierce and Bennett 2009).
documentation.threats:
The Bluespotted Lagoon Ray is caught intentionally and as retained bycatch in artisanal and commercial fisheries in low numbers throughout the Indo-Pacific. It is captured by longline, handline, gill net, trammel net, and harpoons (A. Bin Ali unpubl. data 2020). This species is commonly caught by Bajau Laut in Malaysia and Indonesia using harpoons. This species comprises 2.7% of the rays landed in the markets of Singapore that are captured in either Malaysian or Indonesian waters (N. Clark-Shen pers. comm. 06/05/2020). In the Philippines, this species is one of the most prevalent ray species reported caught in fisheries from 1999 to 2016 across 9 regions (BFAR-NFRDI 2017). Surveys conducted in fish markets in Myanmar have not noted any individuals (A. Maung unpubl. data 2020). This species was reported from Bangladesh in 2011 and 2014, but there have been no records of landings since 2017. This may be due to the small amount of coral reef area in the Bangladesh Exclusive Economic Zone (A. Haque unpubl data 2020). In India, few Bluespotted Lagoon Rays are caught and landed with no individuals being observed in recent years (K.K. Bineesh unpubl. data 2020). 

In the Western Indian Ocean, overall catches reported to FAO have increased over the past 30 years but have levelled off since 1999 suggesting stocks are fully fished. There is concern for serial depletion with the number species landed near-doubling from only 85 in 1971 to 152 reported in 2000 (van der Elst et al. 2005). Artisanal catches are underreported and most small-scale, artisanal, and subsistence coastal fisheries within the Western Indian Ocean are considered to be fully- or overexploited, especially where they are found close to population centres. Over the last ten years, the number of underexploited fisheries in the coastal zone has tended to decline and such fisheries are now an exception (FAO 2006, Pierce et al. 2008).

Global climate change has already resulted in large-scale coral bleaching events with increasing frequency causing worldwide reef degradation since 1997. Almost all warm-water coral reefs are projected to suffer significant losses of area and local extinctions, even if global warming is limited to 1.5ºC (IPCC Report 2019).
documentation.measures:
No specific measures are in place. In the Philippines in 1998, active fishing gears, including trawlers, ‘baby trawlers’, purse seines, and tuna longlines, were prohibited within municipal marine waters (<3 nautical miles from shore). In 1981, there were 5-year closures of the trawl and purse seine fisheries in the waters of Bohol, Cebu, and Negros Oriental and in 1983 in Batangas (Palomares and Pauly 2014, FAO 2020). These bans and closures imply that ‘baby trawlers’ became illegal (Palomares and Pauly 2014). In 1998, a ban was also legislated on "muro ami" gear (an encircling net and pounding devices) and other gear destructive to coral reefs and marine habitats (FAO 2020). Trawlers within commercial waters have been required since 2010 to use Juvenile and Trashfish Excluder Devices under the Fisheries Administrative Order 237 series of 2010. (D. Tanay unpubl. data 2020), which may reduce the retention of larger sharks and rays (Brewer et al. 2006). In the Philippines, there are ~>1,800 Marine Protected Areas (MPAs) (NFRDI 2017, CTI 2020). Some of these MPAs are known to provide shark and ray protection including Donsol, Malapascua, Cagayancillo, and Tubbataha Reefs Natural Park (NFRDI 2017, Murray et al. 2018).

In Indonesia in 1980, trawls were banned, however, large numbers of mini or baby trawls (Lampara) are still used throughout the country (Chong et al. 1987). In 2015, an additional ban on seine nets (Cantrang) was to be fully implemented in February 2020 (Ambari 2019). There are currently plans in place to lift both these bans in the near future (Dharmadi unpubl. data 2020). This species is unlikely to be caught in significant numbers using trawls or baby trawls due to its preference for remaining within the coral reef area that is unsuitable for trawls (Sherman et al. 2018). Within Indonesia there are 196 MPAs making up 239,428 km² that may provide some refuge to this species (CTI 2020). In Malaysia there are 51 MPAs making up 5,462 km² that may provide some refuge to this species (CTI 2020). Most MPAs in the region are not well enforced and unlikely to provide any tangible relief from fishing pressure. Additionally, these MPAs generally allow for fishing by Bajau Laut that target this species. This species is likely spared from trawling and bottom-set nets due to their preference for coral reef habitats in which these gears are not used (Sherman et al. 2018). Further research is needed on population size and trend, and life history, and catch rates should be monitored.
documentation.use_trade: Bluespotted Lagoon Ray meat is used fresh or salted and dried for human consumption throughout most of its range (Last et al. 2010). This is an important species for Bajau Laut in Indonesia and Malaysia, who use this species for local consumption (Noh et al. 2018).
documentation.rationale: The Bluespotted Lagoon Ray (Taeniura lymma) is a small (to 35 cm disc width) stingray with a wide distribution in the Indian and Western Pacific Oceans from South Africa to Papua New Guinea. It is demersal inshore on coral reefs from the surface to a depth of 50 m. The species is a targeted catch of artisanal fisheries and, uncommonly, retained bycatch of commercial fisheries in the Indo-Pacific. It is primarily captured using longline, hardline, gill net, trammel net, and harpoons. Using the Global FinPrint survey data, the population was estimated to have increased over the past three generation lengths (29 years). There is some evidence this increase is related to mesopredator release due to decreasing shark populations. There is no evidence of population decline, and the species is not suspected to be close to reaching the population reduction threshold, therefore, the Bluespotted Lagoon Ray is assessed as Least Concern.
documentation.taxonomic_notes: This species formerly included Teanira lessoni, which is now recognised as a separate species (Last et al. 2016).
